prompt: Which four files does `pyproject.toml` replace?
hint: One built, one installed, one configured, one listed.

choices.text: `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `tox.ini` and `.flake8`, which were where the tools were configured
choices.why: Two of those are tool configuration, and the packaging half is what was replaced.

choices.text: `Pipfile`, `Pipfile.lock`, `poetry.lock` and `uv.lock`
choices.why: Lock files are written per tool and none of them lives in `pyproject.toml`.

choices.text: `requirements.txt`, `requirements-dev.txt`, `constraints.txt` and a lock file
choices.why: Those are all one idea, and a lock file is still a separate file today.

choices.text: `setup.py`, `requirements.txt`, `setup.cfg` and `MANIFEST.in`
choices.why: Each was read by a different program and none of them agreed with the others.

prompt: What makes `[project]` different from `[tool.ruff]`?
hint: One of them is defined somewhere else.

choices.text: `[project]` is defined by a specification; `[tool.<name>]` belongs to whichever tool it names
choices.why: That is why a project declaring itself properly can be handed from one tool to another without an edit.

choices.text: `[project]` is read at install time and `[tool.<name>]` at build time
choices.why: Tool tables are read whenever that tool runs, which is usually neither.

choices.text: `[project]` may appear once and a tool table may be repeated
choices.why: Neither may be repeated, and `[[…]]` is a different construct.

choices.text: `[project]` is required and `[tool.<name>]` is optional in every file
choices.why: Both are optional: a file that only configures `ruff` has no `[project]` at all.

prompt: `[project.scripts]` with `rates = "rates.cli:main"`. What does installing the package do?

choices.text: It makes `python -m rates` work, running `main()` as the module's entry point instead
choices.why: That is `__main__.py`, which is a separate arrangement.

choices.text: It puts a `rates` command on the `PATH` that calls `main()` in `rates.cli`
choices.why: That is how every command-line tool you have installed with `pip` got its name.

choices.text: It marks `main()` as the function the test runner should call first
choices.why: No test runner reads this table.

choices.text: It registers `rates` as an import alias for the `rates.cli` module
choices.why: Import names are not what this table configures.

prompt: Everything under `[______.<name>]` belongs to that program and is ignored by the rest
What does `requires-python = ">=3.11"` buy at install time?

choices.text: The dependency resolver is restricted to packages released after that version
choices.why: Release date has nothing to do with which versions are considered.

choices.text: The package is built separately for each version in the range
choices.why: One wheel covers the whole range unless there is compiled code.

choices.text: `pip` refuses to install on an older interpreter, naming the requirement
choices.why: A better failure than installing and then failing on the first piece of syntax it cannot parse.

choices.text: The interpreter is downloaded if the machine does not have a matching one
choices.why: `pip` installs packages; fetching an interpreter is something `uv` does.

prompt: What is the difference between `[dependency-groups]` and `[project.optional-dependencies]`?
hint: One of them is visible to somebody who installs your package.

choices.text: One is for working on the project; the other is a feature the package advertises
choices.why: Somebody installs an optional set by naming it in brackets. A development group is invisible to them.

choices.text: A group may hold only tools and an optional dependency only libraries
choices.why: Both hold ordinary packages; what differs is who they are for.

choices.text: A group is installed by default and an optional dependency is not
choices.why: Neither is installed by default when somebody installs your package.

choices.text: A group is pinned exactly and an optional dependency carries a range
choices.why: Both take the same specifiers.

prompt: What ships to everybody who installs your library if `pytest` is in the wrong table?
hint: One of the two is part of the interface.

choices.text: A failed install, because `pytest` conflicts with the package's own dependencies
choices.why: There is no conflict; it simply does not belong there.

choices.text: The whole development group, since extras and groups are merged at build time
choices.why: They are separate tables and neither is merged into the other.

choices.text: Nothing — an extra is only installed when it is asked for by name
choices.why: It is only installed when asked for, and it is now advertised as a feature of the package.

choices.text: A test framework, advertised as an optional extra and installable by name
choices.why: Getting the two the wrong way round is the common mistake and this is what it produces.

prompt: `uv sync --no-dev`. What is installed?
hint: One table and not the other.

choices.text: `dependencies` plus any group that is not named `dev`
choices.why: `--no-dev` leaves out the default group, and other groups are selected explicitly.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since `--no-dev` narrows an already empty selection
choices.why: `dependencies` is the selection it is narrowing.

choices.text: Everything in the lock file, since the lock has no concept of a group
choices.why: The lock records which group each package belongs to.

choices.text: `dependencies`, and not one of the dependency groups declared beside them
choices.why: That is what a production install is: the package's own requirements and nothing you needed to work on it.

prompt: Why does a wide `requires-python = ">=3.8"` sometimes hold a library back several versions?
hint: The resolver has to satisfy the whole range.

choices.text: `pip` installs the oldest version compatible with the lowest interpreter named
choices.why: It takes the newest that fits; what constrains it is the range as a whole.

choices.text: Older interpreters have no wheels, so everything is built from source and pinned
choices.why: Building from source does not pin anything.

choices.text: The metadata is rejected by the index for any range spanning four versions
choices.why: The index has no opinion about the width of the range.

choices.text: It has to pick dependency versions that work on every interpreter inside the range
choices.why: A library that dropped 3.8 last year cannot be chosen at all while that bound is there.

prompt: The standard table both uv and Poetry write a development group into: `[______]`
hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.

prompt: `uv add "requests>=2.31"` in a directory with no environment. What does it do?

choices.text: Installs into the interpreter it was run with, since no environment exists yet
choices.why: It refuses to touch the interpreter it was run with and makes an environment.

choices.text: Finds an interpreter, creates `.venv`, resolves, installs, and writes the line into `pyproject.toml`
choices.why: There was no environment to activate first — it made one, in the project directory.

choices.text: Writes the line into `pyproject.toml` and leaves the installing to a later `uv sync` of its own
choices.why: It installs as part of the same command.

choices.text: Fails, asking for `uv venv` to be run first
choices.why: `uv venv` exists and is not required before `uv add`.

prompt: You delete `.venv` and run `uv run main.py`. What happens?

choices.text: It runs against the system interpreter, since there is no environment to prefer
choices.why: It never falls back to the machine's interpreter.

choices.text: It runs after printing a warning that the environment was missing
choices.why: It reports what it installed rather than warning.

choices.text: It fails, since the environment the lock describes is no longer there
choices.why: The lock is what lets it rebuild; nothing is lost by deleting the directory.

choices.text: It rebuilds the environment from the lock and then runs the script, in one command
choices.why: `uv run` checks the environment against the lock first, which is why nothing can be running against a stale one.

prompt: What does `uv sync` do that `pip install -r` cannot?
hint: One verb adds; the other makes equal.

choices.text: Install the development dependencies as well as the runtime ones
choices.why: Two requirements files do that, which is lesson 18's arrangement.

choices.text: Install into an environment that does not exist yet
choices.why: It does that too, and `pip` can be pointed at a fresh environment as easily.

choices.text: Resolve a version range rather than installing an exact pin
choices.why: `pip install -r` resolves ranges all the time.

choices.text: Remove the packages that ought not to be there at all
choices.why: Measured: `uv sync --no-dev` uninstalled five packages, because the set it was asked for does not contain them.

prompt: Which flag belongs in a deployment, and why?

choices.text: `uv sync --frozen`, because it installs from the lock without re-resolving
choices.why: It installs exactly what was tested and cannot resolve to something else on the day the index changes.

choices.text: `uv lock --check`, because it proves the lock and the file agree
choices.why: That belongs in CI; it installs nothing.

choices.text: `uv sync --no-dev`, because production has no use for the development group
choices.why: Also right, and it does not stop a re-resolution.

choices.text: `uv add --frozen`, because a deployment should add nothing
choices.why: A deployment runs no `add` at all.

prompt: `uv lock --check` prints `the lockfile at uv.lock needs to be updated`. What has happened?

choices.text: Somebody changed `pyproject.toml` and did not relock
choices.why: That is exactly the pull request this check exists to fail.

choices.text: The lock was written by a different version of `uv`
choices.why: A version bump of the tool is reported differently.

choices.text: The environment has drifted from what the lock describes
choices.why: That is what `uv sync` fixes, and it is a different comparison.

choices.text: A dependency released a new version inside a declared range
choices.why: The lock stays valid; it names the version that was chosen.

prompt: `poetry install` on an application answers `No file/folder found for package rates`. Why?
hint: Poetry assumes something about the project.

choices.text: The project name and the directory name differ, which Poetry requires to match
choices.why: They may differ, and `packages` is how you say so.

choices.text: It assumes the project is a package to be built, and there is no `rates/` to install
choices.why: For a web service, a script or a data pipeline there is nothing to install, and `package-mode = false` says so.

choices.text: The `src/` layout hides the package, which Poetry does not look inside
choices.why: It looks in `src/` as well; the error is that there is no package at all.

choices.text: The lock file is missing, so there is nothing describing what to install
choices.why: A missing lock produces a different message and is resolved by locking.

prompt: Where does Poetry put its virtual environment by default?

choices.text: In the interpreter's own `site-packages`, with a prefix per project
choices.why: It creates a real virtual environment rather than a prefix.

choices.text: In a central cache, named after the project path and a hash of it
choices.why: `poetry env info -p` prints the path. `uv` puts `.venv` in the project instead.

choices.text: Wherever `VIRTUAL_ENV` points, falling back to the project directory
choices.why: It creates its own rather than adopting one.

choices.text: In `.venv` inside the project, like every other tool
choices.why: That is what `virtualenvs.in-project true` switches it to.

prompt: Poetry 2 writes `[project]`. What does that change?

choices.text: The old `[tool.poetry]` tables are rejected, so old projects have to migrate
choices.why: They still work; conversion is mechanical and not forced.

choices.text: `^` becomes a valid specifier for every tool, since Poetry's syntax is standard now
choices.why: `^` is Poetry's and does not appear in a `[project]` table.

choices.text: The two tools now produce very nearly the same `pyproject.toml`, on the same commands
choices.why: Measured on the same two commands, the files differ in about four lines: parentheses, an upper bound, and a `[build-system]` table.

choices.text: Poetry can now read a `uv.lock`, since both use the same metadata
choices.why: The lock formats are unrelated and neither reads the other's.

prompt: What is the `uv` equivalent of `poetry install --only main`?

choices.text: `uv install --main`, which is the direct translation of the words
choices.why: `uv` has no `install` subcommand of that shape.

choices.text: `uv sync --frozen`, which installs exactly what the lock names
choices.why: That controls re-resolution rather than which groups are chosen.

choices.text: `uv run --no-dev`, which runs without the development packages
choices.why: `uv run` runs a command; the selection is made by the sync.

choices.text: `uv sync --no-dev`
choices.why: The verbs differ and the file does not, which is most of this section.

prompt: Tell Poetry your project is an application rather than a package: `package-mode = ______`
A repository has a `pyproject.toml` and nothing else. What does that tell you?

choices.text: That it predates lock files, and the dependencies are ranges
choices.why: Nothing about the file says when it was written.

choices.text: That it is a package rather than an application, since applications need no metadata
choices.why: Applications declare their dependencies in it as well.

choices.text: That it is managed by `uv`, which is the only tool that needs no lock
choices.why: `uv` writes a lock and commits it.

choices.text: Almost nothing — it might be managed by any of them, or by none
choices.why: A project that only uses it to configure `ruff` has one too. The lock file is what settles it.

prompt: `^2.31` in a dependency list. What is it and what does it mean?

choices.text: A shorthand for an exact pin, used where a lock file is absent
choices.why: It is a range rather than a pin.

choices.text: A standard specifier, equivalent to `~=2.31` in every tool
choices.why: `~=2.31` is the standard form; `^` is not standard at all.

choices.text: A `uv` extension, meaning the newest version at lock time
choices.why: `uv` does not define it either.

choices.text: Poetry's own syntax for a range, meaning `>=2.31,<3`
choices.why: It does not appear in a `[project]` table and `pip` does not understand it.

prompt: You clone a repository with `poetry.lock` in it. What do you run?
hint: Use the tool that wrote it.

choices.text: `poetry install`
choices.why: Running the other tool writes a second lock file that somebody has to delete.

choices.text: `pip install -r requirements.txt`, generated from the lock first
choices.why: That is a migration rather than a way to work on the project.

choices.text: `uv sync`, which reads any lock format and is faster
choices.why: It reads its own and would write a second one.

choices.text: `poetry lock` first, since a cloned lock may be stale
choices.why: Relocking on arrival is how you end up committing an upgrade nobody asked for.

prompt: What does `[build-system]` name?

choices.text: The index the build dependencies are fetched from
choices.why: The index is configured elsewhere.

choices.text: The interpreter the package will be compiled against
choices.why: Compilation targets come from the wheel tags rather than from here.

choices.text: The backend that turns the source into a wheel
choices.why: A project can be managed with `uv` and built with `hatchling`, or managed with Poetry and built with `poetry-core`.

choices.text: The tool that manages dependencies day to day
choices.why: That is independent of it, which is the point of this section.

prompt: What is wrong with adding a `uv.lock` to a repository that already has a `poetry.lock`?

choices.text: Git cannot merge two generated files in the same directory
choices.why: It merges them as badly as it merges one, and that is not the objection.

choices.text: The two formats conflict and `uv` refuses to write beside a `poetry.lock`
choices.why: It writes happily, which is the problem.

choices.text: The versions they pin would have to be identical, which is not achievable
choices.why: They would usually be identical; the problem is that nobody knows which is read.

choices.text: Nobody finds out which is being used until a deployment differs from a laptop
choices.why: Propose a migration as a conversation rather than as a commit.

prompt: What does a lock file contain that `pyproject.toml` does not?
hint: It is longer for a reason.

choices.text: The order the packages must be installed in, worked out by the resolver
choices.why: Install order is recomputed and not recorded.

choices.text: Every transitive package, at one exact version, with the hash of the file
choices.why: Two hundred lines for a project with one dependency and one development tool.

choices.text: The specifiers, resolved into the narrowest range that still satisfies them
choices.why: It holds exact versions rather than ranges.

choices.text: The development groups, which `pyproject.toml` deliberately leaves out
choices.why: `pyproject.toml` declares the groups; the lock records what they resolved to.

prompt: How do you resolve a merge conflict in a lock file?

choices.text: Keep your side, since your environment is the one that was tested
choices.why: That discards whatever the other side added.

choices.text: Merge it line by line, keeping the newer version of each package
choices.why: That produces a set nobody resolved and hashes that may not match.

choices.text: Take the other side's `pyproject.toml` and then regenerate the lock from it
choices.why: A hand edit is the one thing that breaks the guarantee, because the hashes stop matching what the versions claim.

choices.text: Delete it and let the next install write a fresh one
choices.why: Deleting it loses the pins from both sides at once.

prompt: `uv lock --upgrade` against `uv lock --upgrade-package requests`. Which belongs in a routine pull request?
hint: Think about the diff somebody has to read.

choices.text: The second, because moving one package at a time is a small and reviewable change
choices.why: Upgrading everything is a diff nobody reads, and it belongs in a pull request of its own with the tests run against it.

choices.text: Neither, since a lock should only change when `pyproject.toml` does
choices.why: Then security fixes in transitive packages would never arrive.

choices.text: The first, because a partial upgrade leaves the lock internally inconsistent
choices.why: A single-package upgrade resolves the whole graph and stays consistent.

choices.text: Either, since both produce the same result within the declared ranges
choices.why: One moves one package and the other moves all of them.

prompt: What is the difference between `install` and `sync`, stated precisely?
hint: One is a subset relation and the other is equality.

choices.text: `install` reads `pyproject.toml` and `sync` reads the lock file
choices.why: Both read the lock when there is one.

choices.text: `install` makes sure the file's contents are present; `sync` makes the environment equal to the file
choices.why: The difference is a dependency somebody deleted three months ago that is still installed on one machine.

choices.text: `install` works on a package and `sync` on an application
choices.why: Neither cares which the project is.

choices.text: `install` resolves and `sync` uses whatever is already resolved
choices.why: Both can do either, depending on the flags.

prompt: Why is the lock file committed?

choices.text: So that two installs, on two machines, produce exactly the same bytes
choices.why: `pyproject.toml` says `requests>=2.31`, which was true of 2.31.0 in March and is true of 2.34.2 today; the lock says which.

choices.text: So that the resolver can be skipped, which is what makes `sync` fast
choices.why: Speed is a consequence rather than the reason.

choices.text: So that an install works without reaching the index
choices.why: The files still have to be fetched; the lock records which ones.

choices.text: So that a reviewer can see which ranges were declared
choices.why: The ranges are in `pyproject.toml`, which is the reviewable file.

prompt: What is the argument for the `src/` layout?
hint: Think about what a test imports.

choices.text: It keeps the tests and the package in separate directories, which git merges better
choices.why: `tests/` is separate in both layouts.

choices.text: The project root is off `sys.path`, so a test imports the installed copy
choices.why: The tests then exercise what a user gets, rather than the directory sitting beside them.

choices.text: It shortens the import paths, since `src` is stripped from the package name
choices.why: `src` was never part of the package name.

choices.text: It is required by `hatchling`, which does not look for a package at the root
choices.why: Backends support both layouts.

prompt: What does `[build-system]` make possible?
hint: Without it, one command does not know what to do.

choices.text: Publishing to an index, which needs the table and not building
choices.why: Publishing uploads what was built, which needs the table.

choices.text: `pip install -e .` only, since a normal install needs no backend
choices.why: Both go through the backend.

choices.text: Declaring the dependencies, which the backend reads from it
choices.why: Dependencies are declared in `[project]`.

choices.text: `pip install .` — it names the backend that turns the source into a wheel
choices.why: `hatchling`, `setuptools`, `poetry-core` and `flit` all do it, and for a straightforward package the choice barely matters.

prompt: `rates-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl`. What do the three middle parts say?

choices.text: Other environments on the machine see the edit as well

prompt: The two artefacts a build produces are the wheel and the source distribution, or `______`
What has stayed the same across every tool named in this lesson?

choices.text: The command names, which all of them inherited from `pip`
choices.why: The verbs are the same ideas under different names, which is the point.

choices.text: The lock file format, which every tool has agreed on since it was standardised
choices.why: There are four formats for one idea and none of them reads another's.

choices.text: The environment's location, which has been `.venv` in the project throughout
choices.why: Poetry keeps its environments in a central cache.

choices.text: The `[project]` table, and the verbs: add, resolve, lock, sync, run

prompt: A project works, is on Poetry, and `uv` is faster. What does this lesson say to do?

choices.text: Migrate, since a repository on an older tool is one nobody new will know
choices.why: Both are common and both are readable; the migration is the expensive part.

choices.text: Run both, and keep the faster one when the results agree
choices.why: Running both writes two locks and proves nothing.

choices.text: Leave it — a migration costs a day and a class of deployment bug, and the speed saves seconds
choices.why: The current tool is for a new project; the cost of being on the old one is paid later, by whoever joins.

choices.text: Migrate the lock file and keep the rest, so the two can be compared

prompt: Why does the lesson say to be suspicious of an undated packaging tutorial?

choices.text: The specifications change, so older advice describes a file that no longer parses
choices.why: The file has been the stable half; it is the tools that moved.

choices.text: An undated tutorial cannot be checked against the version you have installed
choices.why: You can check it against what you have; the problem is knowing that you should.

choices.text: Half the packaging advice is correct for a year that has passed, and none of it says which
choices.why: Every row of the sequence in this section was the sensible recommendation while it lasted.

choices.text: Packaging tutorials are usually written by tool authors, so they are partial
choices.why: Many are, and that is a different objection.

prompt: What is the honest caveat this lesson puts on its own recommendation?

choices.text: `uv` is the newest of them and is owned by one company, and the last three answers were good too

prompt: Which of these is the thing to learn, according to this section?

choices.text: The file
choices.why: `[project]` is a specification and it will outlive whatever you install this week.

choices.text: The command names, since they are what you type every day
choices.why: They differ per tool and are the part that transfers least.

choices.text: The fastest tool, since the others will converge on what it does
choices.why: The last three answers were also the fastest on the day.

choices.text: The lock format, since reproducibility is what all of this is for
choices.why: The lock format changes with the tool, which is what makes a migration a migration.

prompt: You clone a repository. `ls` shows `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `requirements.txt`. What do you run?

choices.text: `poetry install`, since `pyproject.toml` is Poetry's file
choices.why: It is a standard file that every tool reads.

choices.text: Both, so the environment satisfies each of the two files
choices.why: That is two answers to one question, resolved by neither.

choices.text: `pip install -r requirements.txt`, which needs no tool to be installed first
choices.why: It installs something, and what it installs is not what the lock describes.

choices.text: `uv sync`
choices.why: `uv.lock` means `uv`, and the `requirements.txt` is probably an export somebody keeps for a deployment.

prompt: A pull request adds a dependency to `pyproject.toml` and does not touch `uv.lock`. What fails, and where?

choices.why: That is the outcome the check exists to prevent.

choices.text: The build, since `pyproject.toml` and the lock have to be committed together
choices.why: Nothing enforces that without the check.

choices.text: `uv sync` on the next machine, which resolves the new dependency anyway

choices.text: `uv lock --check` in CI

prompt: The uv command that installs from the lock without resolving again: `uv sync --______`
`dependencies = ["requests (>=2.31)"]` with parentheses. Which tool wrote it?
hint: One of them writes them and the other does not.

choices.text: Either — the parentheses are required by the specification
choices.why: They are optional, which is why the two tools differ.

choices.text: `uv`, which parenthesises to keep the TOML unambiguous
choices.why: It writes the bare form.

choices.text: `pip freeze`, exporting a `pyproject.toml` from an environment
choices.why: `pip freeze` writes `requirements.txt` lines, not a TOML table.

choices.text: Poetry
choices.why: `uv` writes `"requests>=2.31"`. Both are valid and both are read by either tool.

prompt: An environment has a package the lock does not mention. Which command removes it?
hint: One verb makes the environment equal to the file.

choices.text: `uv run`, which rebuilds the environment before each command
choices.why: It checks the environment against the lock and is not how you would do this deliberately.

choices.text: `uv lock`, which rewrites the lock to describe the environment
choices.why: The lock is generated from `pyproject.toml` rather than from the environment.

choices.text: `uv sync`
choices.why: `install` makes sure the file's contents are present; `sync` makes the environment equal to it.

choices.text: `uv remove`, which takes the package out of the project
choices.why: The package is not in the project, which is why it is unmentioned.

prompt: Where does `pytest` belong for a library you publish?

choices.text: In `project.optional-dependencies`, under a `test` extra
choices.why: That advertises a test framework as a feature of your library.

choices.text: In `[build-system].requires`, since the tests run before the wheel is built
choices.why: That table is for what builds the package.

choices.text: In a dependency group, which is invisible to whoever installs it
choices.why: It is invisible to anybody who installs the package, which is what you want.

choices.text: In `dependencies`, since the tests are part of the source distribution
choices.why: Then everybody who installs the library installs `pytest` too.

prompt: Which of these files is edited by a person?

choices.text: `uv.lock`, when a transitive version has to be held back
choices.why: That is `--upgrade-package` or a constraint, not an edit.

choices.text: `pyproject.toml`, which is where the decisions a person makes are written
choices.why: The lock is generated, and a hand edit is the one thing that breaks its guarantee.

choices.text: Both, since the lock records decisions a person makes
choices.why: The decisions go in `pyproject.toml` and the lock records the resolution.

choices.text: `poetry.lock`, to resolve a merge conflict line by line
choices.why: A conflict is resolved by regenerating.

prompt: A project is managed with `uv` and `[build-system]` says `hatchling`. Is that a mistake?
hint: The two tables answer different questions.

choices.text: Yes — a `uv` project has to use `uv_build` for the lock to be valid
choices.why: The lock has nothing to do with the build backend.

choices.text: Yes — `uv` builds with its own backend and the table should name it
choices.why: `uv` has no backend of its own and calls whatever is named.

choices.text: Only for a library; an application may name any backend
choices.why: An application often needs no `[build-system]` at all.

choices.text: No — the day-to-day manager and the build backend are independent of each other
choices.why: `[build-system]` names what turns the source into a wheel, and `uv` is happy to call it.

prompt: Poetry 2 and `uv` were each given the same two commands. How far apart are the two `pyproject.toml` files?

choices.text: A whole table each, since Poetry still writes `[tool.poetry.dependencies]`
choices.why: Poetry 2 writes `[project]`, which is the change this lesson is about.

choices.text: About four lines apart, measured on exactly the same two commands
choices.why: The parentheses, the upper bound Poetry added to `pytest`, and the `[build-system]` table it wrote.

choices.text: Nothing — the two files are byte for byte identical
choices.why: They differ in the three places named above.

choices.text: Most of the file, since the group syntax has no standard form yet
choices.why: `[dependency-groups]` is standard and both write it.

prompt: `^3.11` appears in a file you have been asked to convert. What does it become?

choices.why: `^` is Poetry's. It does not appear in a `[project]` table and `pip` does not understand it.

choices.text: >=3.11,<3.12, since the caret pins the minor version
choices.why: That is `~3.11` in Poetry's syntax.

choices.text: ==3.11, since a caret on an interpreter version means exactly that one
choices.why: It is a range in every reading.

choices.text: ~=3.11.0, which is the standard spelling of the same rule
choices.why: That means `>=3.11.0,<3.12`. The two-component `~=3.11` happens to match here and `~=3.11.0` does not.
